web_evidence.title: The Yearling | Official Publisher Page
web_evidence.note: Simon & Schuster’s sustained Chapter I excerpt narrates Jody as “he” and reports his thoughts and perceptions without a participating narrator.

web_evidence.title: Fanaticism, Yes! Literary Fan Cultures of the Early Twentieth Century
web_evidence.note: Alexandra Edwards’s University of Georgia doctoral dissertation explicitly analyzes The Yearling’s narration as third-person limited and closely aligned with Jody’s consciousness, including discussion of the ending.

web_evidence.title: Glencoe Literature Library Study Guide for The Yearling
web_evidence.note: The McGraw-Hill study guide explicitly identifies the novel’s point of view as third person and structurally explains shifts among Jody’s thoughts, Penny’s thoughts, and detached narration across chapters.

web_evidence.title: The Yearling Teacher Guide
web_evidence.note: The Novel Units curriculum guide explicitly lists the book’s point of view as third person and summarizes sections through Chapters 32–33.

web_evidence.title: Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings Writing Styles in The Yearling
web_evidence.note: The point-of-view section explicitly calls the narrator omniscient and third person, primarily focused through Jody while also accessing other characters.

person_note: The controlling narrator is nonparticipating and narrates Jody, Penny, Ma Baxter, and others in third person, frequently entering their thoughts through free-indirect or omniscient narration. The quotes repeatedly expose this position across scenes, and the authorized opening plus whole-book structural sources agree. Sources vary between calling the technique limited and omniscient because focal access shifts, but both descriptions support THIRD under this methodology. Dialogue is local material; q00222 is a clipped first-person utterance with lost boundaries and provides no evidence of an alternating strand. No credible frame, epistolary, first-person, second-person, or alternating structure was found.
